newsitem.title: CHINA: China CB issue aimed at curbing stock speculation.
newsitem.headline: China CB issue aimed at curbing stock speculation.

text.p: China said on Friday its plans to create a new market in convertible corporate bonds were aimed partly at curbing speculation on the stock markets, but analysts said the markets were nowhere near saturation.

Official media on Thursday reported that the country's top state enterprises could soon apply to issue convertible bonds, with a total value of four billion yuan, pushing them towards eventual listings on the stock markets.

"The convertible bond issue is one of the means the administration is using to adjust the stock markets which have been rising since late December," the official China Securities newspaper said in a front-page commentary on Friday.

The bond issues, the first time China has experimented on a large scale with convertible bonds, come on top of a quota of 10 billion yuan of new domestic A share issues approved at the end of last year.
"The heavy A share issues, and the early May 10 deadline for applications for firms to issue convertible bonds indicate that the financial markets will expand very quickly," the newspaper said.
"It is very important for those who have their eyes only on the stock markets to remember that the convertible bond issue is a sign that market expansion will be quickened," it added.

But stock analysts said the size of the issue and the delay in the availability of bonds for public listing, coupled with the voracious appetite of Chinese investors for stocks means the convertible bond issue could have little market impact.
"I don't think it will have a material impact on the market," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "Four billion is pretty small."
"It might help to calm the markets down, but on the B shares, we're impatient because there's not enough companies coming out and listing," said another Shanghai-based analyst.
"New listings on the A share market are sprouting like mushrooms, but the supply still seems to be small.
"Everything seems to point to people being eager to see more new companies," she said.

Stock prices on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges have risen more than 40 percent since late last year on the back of investor optimism about China's economy and expected improvements in the performance of listed firms, analysts said.
Since Monday, all major Chinese financial newspapers have issued sternly-worded editorials warning that the stock markets are in danger of becoming overheated and too speculative.
But the markets have so far responded little to the warnings. The indices have fallen only slightly with investors believing the market's fundamentals are solid, analysts said.

A new set of rules on convertible bonds issued on Thursday by China's State Council, the cabinet, said the bonds could be issued only by listed companies and designated key state-owned enterprises that meet certain criteria.
Companies must have made a profit in each of the past three years and have an average net asset-profit ratio of more than 10 percent during that period, the rules said.
But for listed firms in the energy, raw materials, and infrastructure sectors, the net asset-profit ratio can be lowered to seven percent.

The rules also say that firms' assets-liabilities ratio must not be higher than 70 percent following a convertible bond issue and that the accumulated outstanding bond volume must not exceed 40 percent of net asset value.

The bonds will have a duration of no less than three years and no more than five years. Each issue must be at least 100 million yuan and the bonds must not carry a coupon rate exceeding the interest rate on bank deposits of a similar duration.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
